title: Data Modeling: Star, Snowflake, Data Vault and the Medallion Layers

concepts.heading: Star Schema: Facts in the Middle, Flat Dimensions Around
concepts.body: A star schema has one central fact table and several dimension tables around it. The fact table records business events at one chosen grain, for example one row per order line, and holds the numeric measures that are summed or averaged (amount, quantity) plus foreign keys to the dimensions. Each dimension holds the descriptive attributes used to filter and group (product name, store city, month) and is denormalized into a single flat table. The analyst test for placing a column is simple: if the query aggregates it, it is a measure in the fact table; if the query slices or labels by it, it belongs in a dimension. A report needs one join per dimension, which keeps SQL short and BI tools happy. When several facts, such as sales and returns, share the same product and date dimensions, those are conformed dimensions, and both facts can be reported side by side with identical labels. Databricks documentation notes that star schemas perform well because queries have few joins.

concepts.heading: Snowflake Schema and Why Databricks Avoids Heavy Normalization
concepts.body: A snowflake schema normalizes the dimensions of a star: a product dimension is split into product, category and department tables, each linked to the next by a key. The benefit is less repeated text and a hierarchy that is maintained in one place, so renaming a category touches one row. The cost is more joins for every query that needs a higher level of the hierarchy, which makes SQL longer and can slow it down. Databricks documentation says star and snowflake schemas both perform well, because standard queries have fewer joins and fewer keys to keep in sync, and because more fields in one table let the optimizer skip data using file-level statistics. It recommends against a heavily normalized third normal form model for new lakehouses. Primary and foreign key constraints in Unity Catalog are informational and not enforced, so duplicates raise no error, yet they document the model, and Genie Agents save defined keys as join relationships.

concepts.heading: Data Vault: Built for Integration and History
concepts.body: The Databricks documentation has no page on data vault, so this lesson uses the widely accepted definitions of the technique. A data vault integrates data from many source systems while keeping full history and the source of every record. It has three table types. Hubs store the unique business keys, such as customer id. Links store the relationships between hubs, such as a customer placed an order. Satellites store descriptive attributes with load timestamps and record source, so each change adds a new satellite row and a new attribute means a new satellite. The table names (hub_customer, link_customer_order, sat_customer_details) give the pattern away. A vault is good at auditability and absorbing change, but it is awkward for dashboards, because answering a business question needs many joins. A common design therefore keeps a data vault as the integration layer and publishes star schemas on top of it for analysts and BI tools.

concepts.heading: Aligning Models with the Medallion Architecture
concepts.body: The medallion architecture organizes data into layers of increasing quality: bronze (raw), silver (validated) and gold (enriched). Following it is a recommended practice, not a requirement. Bronze lands data in its original state with minimal validation, is appended over time and keeps full history. It is meant for workloads that build silver, not for analysts. Silver holds cleansed, deduplicated, schema-enforced data and is where modeling starts; it always keeps at least one validated, non-aggregated version of each record, which is why a data analyst goes to silver for record-level investigations. Gold holds aggregated data tailored to reporting and is where dimensional models, star schemas and weekly aggregates belong, optimized for dashboards. Databricks does not recommend writing to silver straight from ingestion, because schema changes or corrupt records would make the pipeline fail. Because bronze keeps the raw history, a wrong silver rule is fixed by recomputing silver from bronze and then refreshing gold.

examPoints: Fact table = events, measures and foreign keys at one grain; dimension = descriptive attributes. Star has flat dimensions and fewer joins; snowflake normalizes them for less repetition and more joins.
Data vault (hubs, links, satellites) is for integrating many sources with history and audit; the documentation has no page on it. Publish a star schema on top for dashboards.
Medallion mapping: bronze raw, silver validated record level (analyst deep dives), gold aggregated dimensional models for BI. Fix a bad silver rule by reprocessing from bronze.

quiz.q: A retailer keeps a sales fact table joined to flat product, store and date tables. The data team then splits the product table into product, category and department tables. What is the main trade-off of this change?
choices: Fewer joins in every query, because each hierarchy level has its own small table
Less repeated descriptive text and easier hierarchy maintenance, but more joins in queries
Enforced referential integrity, because the new tables are linked by primary and foreign keys
Better audit history, because every table now stores load timestamps for each change
quiz.explain: Splitting a dimension into linked tables turns a star schema into a snowflake schema. It reduces repeated text and lets a category be renamed in one row, but queries that need higher hierarchy levels need extra joins. Primary and foreign keys are informational in Unity Catalog, and load timestamps belong to data vault satellites.

quiz.q: Executives need fast dashboards on revenue by region, and analysts occasionally need individual validated transactions. Where in a medallion design do these two needs belong?
choices: Both in bronze, because it holds the complete raw history of every transaction
Dashboards on silver and investigations on bronze, because bronze is the validated layer
Dimensional models in silver, because gold only stores copies of the raw files
Dashboards on aggregated gold tables, and record-level investigations on silver tables
quiz.explain: Gold holds aggregated, business-ready dimensional models optimized for dashboards, while silver keeps validated, non-aggregated records that analysts use for in-depth analysis. Bronze is raw and meant for the workloads that build silver.

recap: Star = facts plus flat dimensions (few joins), snowflake = normalized dimensions (more joins), data vault = hubs, links and satellites for integration and history. Medallion: bronze raw, silver validated record level, gold aggregated models for BI; fix errors by reprocessing from bronze.

title: Securing Data: Unity Catalog Roles, Privileges, Namespace, Ownership and PII

concepts.heading: Who Can Grant Access: Owners, MANAGE and Admins
concepts.body: Initially users have no access to data in a metastore. Every securable object has exactly one owner, and the creator is its first owner. An owner has all privileges on the object and can grant and revoke access, transfer ownership and drop it. Privileges can be granted by the owner of the object, the owner of the catalog or schema that contains it, a principal with MANAGE on it, or a metastore admin. MANAGE lets an owner delegate administration of one object without handing over ownership. The workspace admin role is not a data administrator role: it manages the workspace and can create catalogs, but granting on an existing object still needs ownership, MANAGE or the metastore admin role, so a permission error on GRANT usually means the wrong role. Databricks best practice is to define groups in the identity provider, sync them to the account, grant privileges to groups and avoid direct grants to users. Then moving an analyst between teams is a single membership change, with no GRANT or REVOKE statements and no stale access.

concepts.heading: Privileges, Inheritance, Views and Functions
concepts.body: Privileges are inherited downward: a grant on a catalog or schema applies to current and future objects below it. Reading a table needs SELECT on the table plus USE SCHEMA on its schema and USE CATALOG on its catalog; the usage privileges alone grant no data access but are a prerequisite. Functions are separate securables: running a SQL function needs EXECUTE, and SELECT does not apply to it. A view is checked against its owner's permissions on the base tables, so on SQL warehouses readers need SELECT on the view and the usage privileges but nothing on the sources. That makes a view a safe way to expose a slice of a table, and it also means the view breaks for everyone if its owner loses access to the sources. By default every catalog of a metastore is reachable from every workspace attached to it; workspace-catalog binding restricts a catalog to chosen workspaces, and access from an unbound workspace fails even with valid grants. BROWSE lets users discover metadata without access to data.

concepts.heading: The Three-Level Namespace
concepts.body: Unity Catalog names objects in three parts, catalog.schema.object, for example retail.sales.orders. A metastore holds catalogs; catalogs are the top container and the typical unit of data isolation; schemas group tables, views, volumes, functions and models. A name with fewer parts is resolved against the current catalog and current schema. If a query on a table shown in Catalog Explorer as retail.sales.orders fails with table not found when written as orders, the fix is to qualify the name or run USE CATALOG retail and USE SCHEMA sales. If neither is set, the workspace default catalog and default schema apply. Because every reference can be fully qualified, one statement can read tables from several catalogs, such as comparing counts in dev.crm.customers and prod.crm.customers with UNION ALL, as long as the user has privileges on both. Tables of the legacy Hive metastore appear as the catalog hive_metastore, for example hive_metastore.default.sales_2019, and can be joined with Unity Catalog tables.

concepts.heading: Ownership, PII Protection and Sharing
concepts.body: Production tables should be owned by groups, not individuals, because refreshes and dashboards that run under a departed owner's identity can break; the creator should reassign ownership. Schema ownership does not pass to the tables created in it, though the schema owner can still grant on them. For personal data the strongest control is not to expose it: build a derived table or view with only the aggregates the audience needs and grant access to that object only. Hiding a column in a chart is presentation, not security. A column mask is applied at query time and users never see the base values, so count(DISTINCT email) on a masked column counts the mask output; analysts should use a non-sensitive key for counts. Managed tables suit regulated data: dropping one lets Databricks delete the data files after a recovery period (7 days by default), while dropping an external table removes only the registration. To share outside the organization, OpenSharing (Delta Sharing) gives read-only access through shares and recipients; Databricks-to-Databricks needs no credential file, while the open protocol serves other platforms.

examPoints: GRANT works for the object owner, the owner of its catalog or schema, a MANAGE holder or a metastore admin; a workspace admin who owns nothing cannot grant. Grant to groups and give production objects to group owners.
Table read = SELECT + USE SCHEMA + USE CATALOG; function = EXECUTE; a view uses its owner's access to the base tables (SQL warehouses); workspace-catalog binding blocks unbound workspaces.

Use catalog.schema.table or USE CATALOG/USE SCHEMA; the legacy Hive tables are hive_metastore.schema.table. For PII expose a derived aggregate; managed tables remove files on drop; share with OpenSharing.

quiz.q: Forty analysts move between three product teams every month. Each team needs SELECT on its own schemas only. Which approach needs the fewest administrative actions?
choices: Grant SELECT on team schemas to a group per team and edit membership in the identity provider
Grant SELECT on each team schema directly to the individual analysts and revoke it again whenever one of them moves
Make each analyst the owner of every team schema so that no grants are needed at all
Grant ALL PRIVILEGES on the catalog to every analyst and rely on team conventions
quiz.explain: Unity Catalog best practice is to grant to groups synced from the identity provider, so a move is one membership change and inherited privileges follow. Direct grants need a GRANT and REVOKE per move, ownership is for administration, and broad grants violate least privilege.

quiz.q: Group finance_analysts has USE CATALOG on corp, USE SCHEMA on corp.utils and SELECT on corp.sales.invoices. A query calling the SQL function corp.utils.net_revenue fails with a permission error. What is missing?
choices: SELECT on the function corp.utils.net_revenue, exactly as for any table or view object
MANAGE on the schema corp.utils, so the group can administer every function in it
EXECUTE on the function, grantable on its schema
Ownership of the table corp.sales.invoices, because the function reads data from that table
quiz.explain: Functions are separate securables and running one needs EXECUTE, plus the usage privileges the group already has. SELECT does not apply to functions, and EXECUTE granted on a schema is inherited by current and future functions in it.

recap: Owners, MANAGE holders, catalog and schema owners and metastore admins grant; use groups and group-owned production objects. Table read = SELECT + usage privileges, function = EXECUTE, view runs with owner access. Names are catalog.schema.object. Protect PII by exposing derived aggregates, prefer managed tables, share with OpenSharing.

title: Final Review: Decision Cheat-Sheet Across the Nine Domains

concepts.heading: Domains 1 to 3 (24 percent): Platform, Managing Data, Importing Data
concepts.body: Platform (11 percent): Catalog Explorer is where an analyst browses catalogs, schemas, tables, views and lineage; certified tables mark trusted datasets, metric views define business measures once, lineage shows upstream sources and downstream consumers, and Marketplace lists shared datasets. Managing Data (8 percent): prefer certified, governed datasets, use tags and lineage to judge fitness, and clean data in SQL by handling NULLs deliberately (IS NULL, coalesce; count(column) skips NULLs while count(*) does not) and filtering invalid rows. Importing Data (5 percent): choose by situation. File upload suits a small local file and creates a table. Auto Loader picks up new files arriving in cloud storage incrementally. Lakeflow Connect provides managed ingestion from supported applications and databases. OpenSharing (Delta Sharing) and Marketplace bring in data another party publishes. When a question describes an analyst with one file and no pipeline skills, the answer is the upload; when it describes a continuous feed of files, it is an incremental ingestion tool.

concepts.heading: Domains 4 and 5 (35 percent): Queries and Query Analysis
concepts.body: Executing Queries (20 percent, the heaviest domain): a SQL warehouse is the compute that runs Databricks SQL; Genie Code helps write and fix SQL. Materialized views store precomputed results that refresh, streaming tables process append-only data incrementally, and a view computes at read time. Managed tables let Unity Catalog control the files, external tables leave them to you. Time travel reads an old state with VERSION AS OF or TIMESTAMP AS OF, and DESCRIBE HISTORY lists commits for audit. Know joins, UNION versus UNION ALL (the latter keeps duplicates), aggregates with GROUP BY, ORDER BY and filters. Analyzing Queries (15 percent): Photon is the vectorized engine, on by default for SQL warehouses, that speeds up SQL workloads, the query profile shows where time goes inside one query, query history lists past runs to find slow or failed statements, and the result cache returns a repeated identical query quickly. Predictive Optimization runs table maintenance automatically, so an analyst does not schedule it by hand. Diagnose first with the profile, then change the query.

concepts.heading: Domains 6 and 7 (28 percent): Dashboards and Genie Agents
concepts.body: Dashboards and Visualizations (16 percent): AI/BI Dashboards are built from datasets and widgets; parameters and filters let viewers change what a chart shows; the visualization type follows the question, such as lines for trends over time, bars for comparing categories and counters for single values. Publishing is a choice between shared data permissions and individual data permissions, where each viewer's Unity Catalog access (including row filters and column masks) decides what they see. Scheduled refresh keeps data current, and with shared data permissions scheduled updates also populate the shared query result cache that speeds up loading for all viewers. Alerts notify when a query result meets a condition. Genie Agents (12 percent): business users ask questions in natural language and Genie generates SQL over the tables the author added. Quality comes from curated tables, clear instructions, example SQL and benchmark questions. Users need access to the agent and also their own data privileges. Fix wrong answers by improving metadata and instructions, not by widening access.

concepts.heading: Domains 8 and 9 (13 percent): Modeling and Securing Data
concepts.body: Data Modeling (5 percent): a star schema is a fact table with flat dimensions and few joins, the snowflake normalizes dimensions at the cost of joins, the data vault (hubs, links, satellites) integrates many sources with history, and Databricks recommends against heavy third normal form. Medallion mapping: bronze raw, silver validated record level, gold aggregated dimensional models for BI. Securing Data (8 percent): grant to groups, let group owners hold production objects, remember that reading a table needs SELECT plus USE SCHEMA and USE CATALOG, running a function needs EXECUTE, and a view uses its owner's access to the base tables. Names are catalog.schema.table. For PII expose a derived aggregate rather than the source, and share externally with OpenSharing. Use the weights to plan the last day: domain 4 alone is a fifth of the exam, and domains 4, 5 and 6 together are 51 percent. When two answers look right, pick the one that solves the stated need with the least privilege and the least engineering.

examPoints: Weights: D4 20, D6 16, D5 15, D7 12, D1 11, D2 8, D9 8, D3 5, D8 5 percent. Spend review time in that order; 45 scored questions in 90 minutes.

Match the situation to the object: materialized view (precomputed, refreshed), streaming table (append-only incremental), view (computed at read), managed table (files removed on drop), external table (files stay).

Read the stem for the decision: least privilege, group grants, diagnose with the query profile before rewriting, fix Genie with metadata and instructions, and shape data with a medallion layer that matches the audience.

quiz.q: A dashboard author needs viewers to see only the regions their own Unity Catalog row filters allow. Which publishing choice fits?
choices: Publish with shared data permissions, so every viewer sees exactly what the author can see
Publish with individual data permissions, so each viewer's own access decides
Publish with a scheduled refresh, which applies the row filters separately for each viewer
Publish with a parameter widget that lets viewers pick only their own region from a list
quiz.explain: With individual data permissions each viewer's Unity Catalog access applies, including row filters and column masks. Shared permissions use the author's access, a schedule only controls freshness, and a parameter is a convenience that does not enforce security.

quiz.q: A query on a SQL warehouse became slow last week, and the analyst wants to know why before changing it. What is the best first step?
choices: Rewrite every join as a subquery and compare the run time by trial and error
Convert the source table to an external table to speed up the file reads
Create a materialized view over the table before looking at the statement
Open the query profile from query history to see where time goes
quiz.explain: The query profile, reached from query history, shows where time is spent inside a statement, so the fix targets the real bottleneck. Rewriting blindly, changing the table type or adding a materialized view are guesses made before diagnosis.

recap: Final pass: heaviest domains first (D4 20, D6 16, D5 15, D7 12). Pick the object or tool that fits the stated need with least privilege and least engineering: upload vs Auto Loader, materialized view vs streaming table vs view, individual vs shared dashboard permissions, profile before rewrite, groups for grants and ownership.
